item.title: Exploring Fault Injection Attacks on HQC and BIKE Beyond Fujisaki-Okamoto Verification
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2492
Authors: Thales B. Paiva, Lucas C. Cardoso, Keerthi Kamalakshan, Hariprasad Valsaraj Kelassery, Marcos A. Simplicio Jr., Shivam Bhasin
Summary: Fault injection attacks have been extensively studied in the context of post-quantum cryptography, yet existing analyses on code-based KEMs largely focus on faults targeting the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform. This work presents new fault injection attacks against BIKE and HQC that operate beyond this commonly protected component and target less obvious instructions within the decapsulation process. The proposed attacks achieve full key recovery using only valid ciphertexts under NIST Level 1 parameters, requiring 17392 and approximately 3 million decapsulation queries for HQC and BIKE, respectively. In addition, we introduce a general approach to identify effective fault locations by analyzing decoder behavior under perturbed conditions. The attacks are experimentally validated on an STM32H7 microcontroller using laser fault injection, demonstrating high repeatability. These results reveal a broader attack surface and provide a foundation for more efficient fault attack analyses in future work.

item.title: Shift-Invariant Permutations with Polynomial Composition: Construction and Algebraic Structure
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2491
Authors: Cheng Lyu, Dabin Zheng, Mu Yuan, Lei Hu
Summary: Shift-invariant permutations of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) are particularly attractive in symmetric cryptography because of their regularity and implementation efficiency. Constructing such permutations with an explicit algebraic structure remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we study a family of shift-invariant transformations of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) constructed from a recursively defined sequence of mappings \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge 0}\) associated with landscapes. First, we prove that, under an explicit dimension condition relating \(n\) to the support of the landscape, the sequence \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge 0}\) has the polynomial composition property if and only if the corresponding landscape is quasi-conserved on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) with a nonzero special index. Then, we determine the eventual zero or periodic behavior of \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge0}\), including the exact index at which the sequence either first vanishes or becomes periodic, together with the least eventual period, and establish linear independence until the first linear relation occurs. When the polynomial composition property holds, we establish an explicit isomorphism between the group of permutation elements in the monoid generated by these mappings and the unit group of a quotient ring \(\mathbb F_2[z]/\langle p(z)\rangle\), where \(p(z)\) is a monomial or a binomial determined by the landscape. This framework reduces the tasks of testing bijectivity, computing iterates, and determining compositional inverses and orders of permutation elements to polynomial computations. Finally, we apply the results to mappings represented by binomials and trinomials in the quotient ring, obtaining explicit criteria and formulas, and tabulate more than one hundred representative constructions of shift-invariant permutations, recovering and unifying several previously studied families.

item.title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2490
Authors: Song Bian, Hyeongmin Choe, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee
Summary: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(\mathcal{H})$ reaction queries, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the entropy of the secret key.
The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side.
We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.

item.title: FAEST on GPUs: Addressing Field Multiplication as a Bottleneck
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2489
Authors: Minseop Choi
Summary: FAEST is a post-quantum signature scheme that combines VOLE-in-the-Head with QuickSilver to prove knowledge of a secret key. It relies on well-established symmetric primitives and offers small public keys, but signing and verification are computationally expensive. We present an NVIDIA GPU implementation of the key-generation core and the QuickSilver procedures OWFProve and OWFVerify for the standard and EM constructions in both s and f variants. Profiling shows that once AES is accelerated by hardware, field multiplication in QuickSilver becomes the largest cost throughout this parameter grid. In FAEST-128f, field multiplication takes about 82% of signing time. To address this bottleneck in our GPU implementation of FAEST, we use PTX clmad for native carry-less arithmetic and Karatsuba to reduce the number of limb products. The clmad build improves throughput across all twelve OWFProve and OWFVerify paths, and its advantage grows with the field width. On an RTX A5000, PTX clmad raises standard OWFProve throughput to 1.99x, 2.45x, and 2.82x that of the software-multiplication build at 128, 192, and 256 bits, respectively. Together, PTX clmad and Karatsuba deliver 26.6x the throughput of the software-multiplication build in the field-multiplication-heavy kernel of standard 256-bit OWFProve. When all OWFProve stages are included, the combined build reaches 2.9x and 3.1x the software throughput for standard and EM at 256 bits, respectively. These results establish native carry-less arithmetic as a key design choice for GPU implementations of FAEST, with Karatsuba providing an additional improvement for 256-bit proving.

item.title: Yoshan: Algebraic-Circuit Co-Synthesis and Search Methodology of Hardware-Efficient S-Boxes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2488
Authors: Robert Hanhan, Binyamin Alony, Itamar Levi
Summary: Choosing an S-box for a hardware-oriented cipher means balancing cryptanalytic quality (differential uniformity $\delta$, linearity $L$, algebraic degree), circuit complexity (the number of AND gates and the AND depth $D$), and implementation cost (silicon area and, in masked designs, registers and fresh randomness). Under Boolean masking the non-linear gates dominate this cost and $D$ sets the latency, so automated S-box searches have concentrated on quadratic permutations, which admit depth-1 circuits but make the algebraic degree of a cipher grow slowly.
We present YOSHAN, a co-synthesis system that optimizes an S-box and its gate-level circuit together instead of fixing the lookup table first. It combines structural algebraic seeding (subfield towers, Feistel, Misty, and product-round Feistel constructions, affine wrappers, CCZ graph automorphisms, bilinear and shear seeds), cryptographically guided evolution of the circuit DAG by algebraic rewrites, a differentiable Piling-Up relaxation with Hungarian LSAP projection, and multi-level circuit optimization (SMT sub-DAG shaving, stage-preserving common-subexpression elimination, exact depth-1 SAT synthesis, and algebraic-structural inverse compilation) inside a quality-diversity archive across $n \in \{5,6,7,8\}$. Every archived circuit is exported gate for gate to SystemVerilog and certified by exhaustive simulation and a Z3 miter. The archive holds 31,129 certified netlists covering 56 $(n,\delta,L,\deg)$ profiles; three extended-affine invariants and an exact affine-equivalence solver split them into members of known classes (Category A) and permutations provably not extended-affine equivalent to any power map or to the cipher S-boxes we compare against (Category B, 15 benchmark classes $\mathsf{YSH}_{n,i}$, 13 with stratified subspace-filtration degree spectra). All 30 reported S-boxes and their explicit inverses are synthesized gate-exactly in 45 nm CMOS, unmasked and as pipelined first-order DOM modules, and every benchmark circuit is traced to its seed and the search stage that shaped it. Results include a gate-exact AES-equivalent circuit at the optimal AND depth $3$ ($42$ AND, $101$ XOR) with an explicit depth-3 inverse ($42$ AND, $106$ XOR), a 6-bit degree-5 permutation $\mathsf{YSH}_{6,5}$ ($\delta=6$, $L=24$, boomerang uniformity $\beta=14$) with $12$ AND gates, a 5-bit quartic permutation $\mathsf{YSH}_{5,4}$ with $5$ AND gates at depth $2$ in both directions, and 8-bit degree-7 permutations with $28$ and $18$ AND gates. All forward and inverse circuits are compared with the best published implementations.

item.title: A Hybrid BP-SAT Attack on MILENAGE: Combining the Complementary Strengths of Algebraic and Soft-Analytical Side-Channel Attacks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2487
Authors: Elena Dubrova, Sönke Jendral, Linus Backlund, Mats Näslund
Summary: Profiled side-channel attacks combine noisy leakage predictions with the mathematical relations imposed by the target algorithm to recover secrets from a small number of observations. Two established approaches are algebraic side-channel analysis (ASCA), which encodes leakage predictions and algorithmic relations as a Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem, and soft-analytical side-channel analysis (SASCA), which performs probabilistic inference over a factor graph using belief propagation (BP). We evaluate both on the AES-based MILENAGE authentication algorithm deployed on USIM cards, targeting the first AES-128 invocation on $\mathit{RAND}\oplus\mathit{OPc}$ under the subscriber key $K$, where $\mathit{OPc}$ is an operator-specific secret unknown to the attacker. Neural networks predict posterior probability distributions over the AES S-box output byte values across multiple rounds and these predictions are supplied to ASCA and SASCA to recover $K$ and $\mathit{OPc}$ from a single trace. SASCA recovers both secrets in 87.7% of attacks, but converges to an incorrect $\mathit{OPc}$ in 6.1% of cases despite recovering $K$ correctly. ASCA enforces global consistency and resolves this ambiguity, but it succeeds in only 34% of attacks under a 1-hour timeout and our constraint-selection strategy. Motivated by these complementary failure modes, we combine the two into a hybrid attack in which BP refines the neural network predictions before they are supplied to the SAT solver. The hybrid approach recovers both secrets in 93.8% of single-trace attacks, resolving all cases where SASCA recovers $K$ correctly but $\mathit{OPc}$ incorrectly. It has a higher success rate and a lower average runtime than either method alone, despite performing more work per attack. Finally, we suggest a countermeasure, based on masking each AES round key with an independent, per-device secret, that reduces an attacker's advantage over guessing $K$ and $\mathit{OPc}$ to zero bits, and confirm empirically that it defeats the hybrid attack in all evaluated cases.

item.title: Heterogeneous CPU–NPU Implementation of the AIMer Post-Quantum Signature for Low Latency on a Mobile SoC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2486
Authors: Myoungsu Shin, Jihoon Jang, Hanbeom Shin, Insung Kim, Dongjae Lee, Donggeun Kwon
Summary: Signatures in the MPC-in-the-head paradigm rest only on a symmetric primitive, but their signing is slow, because it computes hash functions and a linear map for every simulated party of every repetition. We show that the Hexagon NPU of Snapdragon SoCs shortens one complete signing operation of AIMer, the MPC-in- the-head signature that the Korean post-quantum cryptography competition selected. Prior work speeds up such signatures on one CPU core, accelerates post-quantum arithmetic on GPUs for batches of operations, and reports only single post-quantum functions for mobile NPUs. Our implementation divides each signing operation along its dependency graph. The NPU computes the hashing and the per-party linear map of the last repetitions, which need no secret key, and the CPU keeps the secret key and the two hashes that absorb the repetitions in index order. A fast AArch64 implementation serves both as the CPU part and as the baseline, and it signs 4.5 to 6.1 times faster than the reference implementation on one core. On a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 tablet, one core with the NPU signs 1.30 to 1.42 times faster than two cores and 1.74 to 1.97 times faster than one core for the three short-signature parameter sets. The same configuration uses 13 to 27 % less energy per signing operation than two cores. On Snapdragon 8 Elite and 8 Gen 2 phones, one core with the NPU signs 1.28 to 1.35 and 1.74 to 1.82 times faster than two cores.

item.title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2485
Authors: Valerio Cini, Antonio Guimarães, Russell W. F. Lai, Michał Osadnik, Ivy K. Y. Woo
Summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) allows arbitrary computation over encrypted data, but its secret key presents a single point of failure which limits its applications. Threshold FHE patches this gap by distributing the secret key to $K$ parties, requiring a threshold $t \leq K$ of them to cooperate for decryption. We focus on the asynchronous setting where a ciphertext can be decrypted by collecting decryption shares from any $t$ parties who do not need to coordinate or even be online simultaneously. Asynchronous schemes are sought in applications such as privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual Machines (EVM), processing of long-lived private data with quorum-based decryption and the thresholdisation of any cryptographic primitive in general.
We present Tulva, a practical threshold FHE scheme which equips a base FHE scheme with an asynchronous threshold decryption mechanism in a modular way. Our scheme simultaneously (1) is compatible with virtually any base FHE scheme and leaves its ciphertexts unchanged apart from an appended random tag, (2) supports a wide range of threshold profiles $(t,K)$ and ring degrees $\geq 256$ with 6--25 bits partial decryption per plaintext bit, and (3) achieves security in the presence of partial decryption queries on challenge ciphertexts based on the standard LWE assumption.
We provide an open-source implementation, benchmark its threshold decryption performance and evaluate the end-to-end costs for typical privacy-preserving EVM use cases. For 16-out-of-512 threshold and a publicly preprocessed ciphertext, computing secret-dependent partial decryption and public share combination requires only 3.7ms and 0.5ms, respectively, on commodity hardware. Compared with the state-of-the-art synchronous scheme [Zyskind et al., CCS'25], we replace their ciphertext-independent yet interactive preparation of secret-correlated randomness with a public, ciphertext-dependent 0.5s preprocessing step, eliminate interaction in the online phase while maintaining similar decryption time on the same machine, and support 32$\times$ more total users.

item.title: Unveiling the Cost: Gas-Efficient Output-Private Distributed VRFs on Ethereum
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2484
Authors: Ahmet Ramazan Ağırtaş, Arda Buğra Özer
Summary: Unbiased and publicly verifiable randomness is a fundamen- tal component of Web3 security, and output-private distributed verifiable random functions (DVRFs) extend this guarantee by keeping the gener- ated randomness hidden from chain observers until the requester chooses to reveal it. Two constructions currently realize output privacy under dif- ferent algebraic regimes: FlexiRand, whose on-chain verification rests on bilinear pairings, and IcyVeil, a pairing-free design whose verification re- duces to a constant number of group operations. While it is folklore that pairing-free verification should be cheaper on the Ethereum Virtual Ma- chine (EVM), the actual on-chain cost of output-private randomness has never been measured for either scheme. In this paper, we present the first EVM implementations of both constructions. Both verifiers are served by a single coordinator contract realizing the common blind–evaluate–pre- verify lifecycle, so that every measured difference is attributable solely to the verification arithmetic. The isolated verification is 57% cheaper in execution gas for the pairing-free scheme (51,561 against 118,541 gas); over the full request lifecycle, whose remaining stages are shared, the ad- vantage is about 11%. This on-chain saving comes with a cost off chain: the pairing-free scheme’s distributed evaluation requires roughly 2.5 to 8.2 times more aggregate committee compute across committee configu- rations (n, t), a gap absorbed comfortably by Ethereum’s block time and one that narrows further once the committee executes concurrently. We report both axes, separating one-time distributed key generation (DKG) cost from IcyVeil’s consumable preprocessing, and reconcile the on-chain and off-chain ratios, which point in opposite directions. All contracts, harnesses, and raw measurements are publicly available.

item.title: Uniform Sharing in Multiple Stages: Towards Second-Order Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2483
Authors: Aein Rezaei Shahmirzadi, Artemii Ovchinnikov, Siemen Dhooghe
Summary: Mitigating Side‑Channel Analysis (SCA) of cryptographic implementations relies heavily on masking schemes; however, achieving efficient and straightforward hardware realizations remains challenging. While Threshold Implementation (TI) provides provable security against glitches in hardware, it incurs significant area overhead due to the large number of shares required to protect non‑linear functions. Successor schemes achieve the same security order with a minimal number of shares, but often rely on a high amount of per‑cycle randomness, especially at higher orders. Recent optimizations such as NullFresh and MultiStage attain minimal share counts without additional randomness; however, they lack a generalized methodology for higher‑order security. In particular, although MultiStage enables automated generation of low‑randomness masked designs, it is currently limited to first‑order protection.
In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing an automated masking technique for arbitrary functions that guarantees second‑order security in the glitch‑extended probing model. Building upon the MultiStage approach, our method preserves the efficiency of NullFresh by minimizing requirements for fresh masks, while overcoming structural limitations of previous schemes. We demonstrate the feasibility of the approach on the lightweight block ciphers PRINCE, Midori, and SKINNY. The resulting designs are formally verified using SILVER and PROLEAD, and experimentally evaluated on FPGA using TVLA.

item.title: Edabits Generation with Quasi-Linear Communication Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2482
Authors: Alexander Bienstock, Daniel Escudero, Qijia Fan, Fengrun Liu, Yifan Song
Summary: The work of (Escudero et al., CRYPTO 2020) introduces the so-called edabits, which are defined as a secret sharing of an integer over an arithmetic domain, together with its bit decomposition secret shared over a binary domain. In the same work, it is shown how edabits can be used to securely evaluate advanced primitives such as comparison, bit decomposition, and truncation, which are essential building blocks in more complex applications such as privacy-preserving machine learning and beyond. Edabits are general and can be defined over any secret-sharing scheme or corruption model. Such flexibility, coupled with their wide range of applications, makes edabits a powerful target correlation.
Escudero et al.~introduced a protocol to generate edabits that works in the arithmetic black-box (ABB) model, that is, it is agnostic to the concrete secret-sharing scheme and even works both for fields $\mathbb{F}_p$ and rings $\mathbb{Z}_{2^\ell}$, as well as both for honest majority $t2$ and dishonest majority $t0$. This includes the honest majority case $t2$, but also dishonest majority with an (arbitrarily small) constant fraction of honest parties. Our result is achieved via novel applications of randomness extraction methods, as well as better edabit aggregation for the binary components. Along the way and of independent interest, we improve the communication complexity of dabit generation (dabits are bits shared in both binary and arithmetic domains) from $\Omega(n^2\ell)$ bits achieved in (Rotaru and Wood, INDOCRYPT 2019), to linear $O(n\ell)$ bits.

item.title: Polygero: Proximity Testing From Polynomial Challenges
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2481
Authors: Matteo Frigo, abhi shelat
Summary: We present a new proximity test for Reed--Solomon codes that admits a higher-agreement regime with soundness approaching the field's bit length.
All prior work in this area [AHIV2017,BCIKS2020,BCHKS2025] uses the idea of *scalar* batching in which the verifier provides a scalar challenge for each codeword, and the prover must supply a codeword equivalent to the combination, and the verifier tests it at randomly opened columns.
Our main insight is to instead use a low-degree polynomial challenge for each codeword. We prove that the low-dimensional spaces generated by polynomial challenges become maximum distance separable (MDS) after deleting a few coordinates, and this phenomenon leads to a new kind of proximity gap that we can exploit.
This insight enables a simpler, in fact elementary counting proof for soundness of the proximity tests. We do not need the Polishchuk--Spielman lemma or Guruswami--Sudan decoding.
The same technique proves soundness of Polygero, a Ligero-inspired IOP~[AHIV17], beyond the unique-decoding regime. Through recursion, Polygero produces proofs with a number of field elements logarithmic in the witness size, independently of the number of linear constraints. It does not require roots of unity in the finite field or out-of-domain sampling.
The soundness analysis, including the extractor and the recursive composition, and every reported parameter schedule are machine-checked in Lean.

item.title: Post-Quantum Certificate-Based PSK Provisioning for WireGuard via Mutual TLS, DTLS, and QUIC: Design and Performance Study
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2480
Authors: Che Hang Ng, Emil Künstner, Bastian Küppers, Theodor Schnitzler, Misha Glazunov
Summary: We present an architecture that provides WireGuard’s resistance against future quantum adversaries. By preserving the core protocol, our approach minimizes deployment effort and adds certificate-based identities to WireGuard peers. To achieve Post-Quantum (PQ) resistance, we establish an external mutually authenticated control channel built on the TLS 1.3 handshake and layered on top of TCP, UDP, or QUIC. Its key establishment includes Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM). An auxiliary shared secret is derived from the exported keying material of the resulting session and injected into WireGuard’s native Pre-Shared Key (PSK) interface; this derivation is identical for all three transports. To support scalable deployment, the control channel is authenticated with X.509 certificates issued by a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), using the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) for PQ certificate signing. We develop a Tamarin model of the composition layer and symbolically analyze the secrecy, binding, and provisioning-order properties of the interface between TLS 1.3 handshake and WireGuard, identifying the critical conditions necessary for secure deployment. Finally, we evaluate the design to quantify handshake latency and CPU time for classical, pure PQ and hybrid key establishment, classical and ML-DSA certificates, and the three transports, comparing it against an existing PQ WireGuard baseline achieving state-of-the-art results.

item.title: Committing Security of Forkcipher-based AEAD
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2479
Authors: Samir Kundu, Sougata Mandal, Hrithik Nandi
Summary: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) provides confidentiality and integrity, but traditional security notions do not prevent ciphertexts from decrypting correctly under multiple keys. This motivates committing security, which requires ciphertexts to bind to their encryption inputs uniquely. Recent analyses revealed commitment failures in several forkcipher-based AEAD schemes, leaving open the question of whether these failures are inherent to forkciphers or design specific. We provide a comprehensive committing security analysis of existing forkcipher-based AEAD constructions, filling this gap by establishing both negative and positive results. Our analysis shows that while some designs inherently fail to achieve strong commitment, others achieve meaningful commitment guarantees, demonstrating that forkciphers can serve as a foundation for committing-secure AEAD schemes. We derive tight bounds for commitment notions for existing constructions. As a key technical contribution, we formalize a forkcipher-based hash construction and prove its collision resistance, which serves as a foundation for our security analysis.

item.title: Hardware-Level Mitigation of Micro-Architectural Leakages in Embedded Processors
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2478
Authors: Niels Wieser, Nicolai Müller, Amir Moradi
Summary: Cryptographic software, with its inherent flexibility and adaptability, has become essential for meeting today’s rapidly evolving security requirements, despite offering lower performance than dedicated hardware accelerators. However, Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) complicates its secure execution on physical hardware, making robust protection a central challenge. While the masking countermeasure offers provable security guarantees in theory, its effectiveness is often undermined by the processor’s micro-architecture. In response, formal adversary models have been adapted to account for micro-architectural leakage under generic (but over-conservative) assumptions on the hardware. Consequently, achieving security under such a generic model requires compilers to produce less performant software. To bridge this gap, secure hardware-software co-design assumes a precisely specified hardware leakage behavior, enabling the specification of constraints for secure compilation. While this approach reduces the overhead required to counteract these effects, it does not entirely remove it. This work follows a more fundamental paradigm: instead of managing leakage in software, we aim at eliminating it at its source. Conceptually, we propose architectural changes to general-purpose processors at the Register-Transfer Level (RTL) that remove the root causes of micro-architectural leakages. The application of these changes enables the secure execution of masked software without introducing micro-architectural leakage under the Robust but Relaxed (RR) d-probing model, thereby removing the need for complex, security-aware compilers and hardware-specific workarounds in the software. While our countermeasures can be applied to many micro-architectures, we formally prove the security of each countermeasure individually and integrate them into the Ibex processor, whose security we evaluate as a whole through tool-assisted leakage assessment of the full netlist and physical experiments on a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA).

item.title: Secret Sharing from Non-Extractable Randomness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2477
Authors: Divesh Aggarwal
Summary: Bosley and Dodis (TCC 2007) proved that a class of imperfect randomness sources that suffices for information-theoretic encryption of messages longer than the logarithm of the key length must admit deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits, and asked whether the same is true of two-out-of-two secret sharing. Aggarwal, Chung, Obremski, and Ribeiro (TCC 2022) gave a positive answer for schemes that are in addition leakage-resilient or non-malleable; the original question remained open.
We answer it in the negative. For every $b\ge2$ we construct a class of flat sources on $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$, each of min-entropy at least $b$, together with a perfectly correct and perfectly private two-out-of-two scheme that shares a $b$-bit secret into two $(b+1)$-bit shares using any source in the class, and we show that every deterministic map from $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$ to $\{0,1\}$ is at statistical distance at least $1/6$ from uniform on some source in the class. This implies that sharing a long enough secret does not require extractable randomness. The proof is a short parity argument. The idea of the construction extends to other thresholds: for two-out-of-$n$ and $r$-out-of-$r$ sharing we give perfect schemes with $(b+1)$-bit shares, private for classes of flat sources from which no single bit can be extracted with error below $1/(4n-2)$ and $1/(2(2^r-1))$, respectively.

item.title: On the Hardness of Finding Permutation Automorphisms of Linear Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2476
Authors: Michele Battagliola, Giuseppe D'Alconzo, Laura Mattiuz, Paolo Santini, Federica Zanetti
Summary: We study the hardness of finding permutation automorphisms of linear codes. We look into three main problems: $\mathsf{AUT}$, $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ which, respectively, ask to find a non-trivial automorphism, a generating set and the order of the automorphism group. We give polynomial time reductions from $\mathsf{AUT}$ to $\mathsf{ISO}$ (the problem of finding a permutation isomorphism between two linear codes), and from $\mathsf{ISO}$ to $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$. This shows that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ are unlikely to be easy in the worst case, since all known solvers for $\mathsf{ISO}$ take exponential time if the hull dimension (the subspace given by the intersection between the code and its dual) is large enough. Furthermore, we give a reduction from $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ to the problem of finding generators for the automorphism group of a graph, which we refer to as $\mathsf{GraphAUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$. Up to some polynomial factors, the reduction runs in time $O(n^{h})$, with $n$ being the code length and $h$ the hull dimension: for $h = O\big(\log(n)\big)$, this implies that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ can be solved in worst case quasi-polynomial time. We also give a simpler version of the reduction, running in time which is exponential in the worst case (arguably, only for rather contrived codes), even for small $h$. However, heuristically, the algorithm is on average extremely efficient for small $h$. We use it as a concrete solver and show that a proof-of-concept implementation is significantly faster than the built-in implementations of Leon's and Feulner's algorithms provided by $\texttt{Magma}$ and $\texttt{Sagemath}$.

item.title: Tamper Sensing Meshes in Payment Terminals and Beyond
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2475
Authors: Jan Sebastian Götte, Björn Scheuermann
Summary: Card Payment Terminals commonly use tamper sensing meshes to deter physical attacks on devices handling sensitive data such as cryptographic keys. Although their use of such meshes is frequently referenced in research literature, the public record contains little research on their construction. Addressing this gap, in this paper we present the first comprehensive analysis of the practical implementation of tamper sensing meshes across a wide range of payment terminals, and some other devices such as ATM key pads and a data center HSM. We provide detailed photos of critical features. Based on our observations, we construct a taxonomy of mesh construction techniques. Our analysis reveals that most commercial devices use surprisingly simple construction techniques, and their structure size rarely approaches manufacturing limits.
Based on our analysis, we identify a concise set of design patterns for the construction of secure tamper sensing meshes. We conclude that designing tamper sensing meshes that exceed the industrial state of the art is viable even using inexpensive and easily available manufacturing processes. Our set of design recommendations creates a foundation for both the practical tamper sensing mesh implementations and for future research into their design. Our results enable researchers to base test specimens on concrete evidence of industrial practice.

item.title: Software-Pipelining The Number Theoretic Transform on Neural Processing Units: A Loop-Fission Methodology
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2474
Authors: Henri Vermeersch, Xander Pottier, Quinten Norga, Thomas de Ruijter, Ingrid Verbauwhede
Summary: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) rely heavily on the number theoretic transform (NTT) for efficient polynomial multiplication. While GPUs and FPGAs have been widely explored for NTT acceleration, neural processing units (NPUs), a rapidly growing class of AI accelerators, remain largely unexplored for cryptographic workloads. In this work, we develop a methodology for accelerating the NTT on NPUs, using AMD’s AI Engine (AIE) architecture as a representative NPU to develop and benchmark it. At its core is manual loop fission, in which large and complex loops are split into smaller primitives, enabling highly efficient software pipelining and avoiding memory stalls or register spilling. Applying it, we develop efficient Barrett reduction primitives and use these to construct three high-throughput, low-latency NTT implementations (radix-2, radix-4, and radix-8), achieving significant performance gains over the AIE compiler and prior literature. On AMD’s first-generation AIE specifically, we achieve speedups of $8.27\times$ to $13.2\times$ in throughput and $2.44\times$ to $10.3\times$ in latency per AIE tile in comparison with prior work. Our implementations support arbitrary NTT-friendly moduli and polynomial sizes up to degree 4096 for 14-bit moduli and 2048 for 30-bit moduli. Finally, we discuss the portability of our techniques to other NPU architectures, and identify which architectural features are most beneficial for NTT acceleration.

item.title: edaBits in the Exponent (edaBitE) and Issuer-Hiding Blind Signatures from ML-DSA and VOLE-in-the-Head
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2473
Authors: Carsten Baum, Marvin Beckmann
Summary: Blind signatures let a user obtain a signature by interacting with an issuer that controls the signing key, while the issuer never sees the message. They form the basis of anonymous credentials, which are the centerpiece of privacy-preserving digital identification to be deployed widely in the coming years. Existing plausibly quantum-secure blind signatures rely on bespoke cryptographic constructions, instead of standardized ones. This is dissatisfying from a cryptographic perspective, and also leads to practical issues: secret signing keys are often stored in secure elements, in which case only signature algorithms supported by certified secure elements can be the basis for deployed protocols.
We give the first blind signature whose issuer runs a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme unmodified. Issuance is just an ML-DSA signature on a commitment, and the blind signature is a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge, using the VOLE-in-the-head zero-knowledge proof system, of the ML-DSA signature. Security reduces to the EUF-CMA security of ML-DSA and to the proof system, with no new assumptions. A blind signature is about $1$ MB and takes under a second to produce and half a second to verify. Issuer-hiding and selective disclosure of signed attributes can easily be added on top for a few tens of kilobytes, at a proof size essentially independent of how many issuers the list names.
Underlying the construction is edaBitE, a novel batch consistency check between binary and prime-field commitments. In a non-interactive proof, the existing edaBits checks it replaces would be the single largest item in the blind signature. We believe that edaBitE is of independent interest.

item.title: Nowhere Man: Device Binding for Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2472
Authors: Calvin Abou Haidar, Ryo Kikuchi, Octavio Perez-Kempner, Marcel Tiepelt
Summary: Anonymous credentials are seeing widespread deployment. Notably, the European Commission plans to roll out age-verification solutions based on anonymous credentials by the end of 2026. Similarly, Google open-sourced Longfellow, a zero-knowledge proof system that lifts the standardized mobile Driver License framework into a full-fledged anonymous credentials, and is currently being integrated with Google Wallet.
Any secure deployment of anonymous credentials must address two major challenges: 1) provide guarantees against credential sharing, and 2) support proof-of-personhood. The standard approach adopted by the industry to address both is device binding, which is mandatory for mDL and was only recently formalized for anonymous credentials by Friedrichs et al. (Eurocrypt '26). Simply put, the idea is to have the user's phone Secure Element sign a fresh challenge from the verifier, and to prove knowledge of this signature in zero-knowledge at each credential presentation.
To date, all existing approaches, including Vega (S&P '26), have only considered non-post-quantum solutions based on legacy signature schemes. Crucial for near-term deployments and adoption is to work with standardized post-quantum signature schemes, such as ML-DSA, which were not designed for privacy. Because of this, solutions based on general non-interactive zero-knowledge proof systems (e.g., Longfellow) appear to be needed. This genericity, however, requires proving complex statements, significantly impacting proving time.
In this work, we present a modular device binding protocol tailored to work with ML-DSA. We avoid the pitfalls of the generic approach by leveraging the structure of ML-DSA resulting in an efficient solution, but retaining the security underlying the post-quantum standard. Our most efficient variants additionally rely on a weak-MLWR assumption for unlinkability, which can be removed at the cost of lower efficiency. While tailored for ML-DSA and requiring no modification to the FIPS~204 signing interface, our solution is modular enough to be integrated with different anonymous credential schemes, allowing real-world solutions to pick the most efficient building blocks. To demonstrate the feasibility of our solution, we provide a proof-of-concept implementation.

item.title: Connecting Cryptanalytic Distinguishers through Divisibility
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2471
Authors: Hosein Hadipour
Summary: Integral distinguishers can reveal more than a zero-sum property: the number of ones in an output component may be divisible by a high power of $2$, rather than merely being even. To exploit this divisibility, we relate linear, integral, differential-linear, and restricted differential sums through two-way conversions with explicit divisibility guarantees and data complexity, recovering established links as special cases. We derive exact random-permutation probabilities and rigorous bounds to quantify the distinguishing strength while accounting for dependencies between output conditions. To discover these properties, we develop automated MILP/SAT models that use complete-round Walsh coefficients or combine Walsh and ultrametric representations to obtain stronger bounds. These weighted models prove finite divisibility even when compatible trails exist, beyond what trail-existence tests alone can establish. For differential-linear sums, we show that combining differential and linear propagation with local DLCT zeros can give false zero-correlation claims. We address this limitation with exact mix-basis models that establish zero correlation and finite divisibility. To complement these symbolic methods, we provide a black-box algorithm using exact histograms and the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to search all output masks for selected input conditions and identify zeros and finite divisibility properties. Our MILP/SAT models significantly improve the divisibility bounds reported by Beyne and Verbauwhede in 674 cases across the SIMON family, as well as for PRESENT, without trail enumeration and at unchanged data complexity, e.g., from $2^5$ to $2^{11}$ on 9-round SIMON32 and from $2^6$ to $2^{22}$ on 10-round SIMON48. To our knowledge, we are the first to prove higher divisibility for 8-round SPECK and for BEANIE, with new bounds for GIFT-64 and Ascon and exact counts for SKINNY-64. Our black-box searches reveal new properties on RC5, ChiLow-32, KeeLoq, and KATAN32, including output-bit combinations missed by single-bit searches, and lead us to introduce probabilistic divisibility.

item.title: Refined Application of the XL Algorithm within the Algebraic Approach to the Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2470
Authors: Hiroki Furue, Yusuke Aikawa
Summary: The Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) is a fundamental mathematical problem underlying code-based cryptography, which is considered a promising candidate for post-quantum cryptography. The Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem (RSDP) is a variant of the SDP in which the error vector follows a specific block-wise structure. Recent developments in RSDP-based cryptographic schemes have led to a wider variety of parameter settings, making it increasingly important to evaluate the complexity of solving the RSDP over a broad range of parameters. One of the main approaches to solving the RSDP is the algebraic approach, which transforms a given RSDP instance into a polynomial system and solves it using algebraic techniques such as the XL algorithm. In this work, we construct and analyze algebraic algorithms for the RSDP by combining and extending techniques used in existing algebraic approaches. Our algorithms mainly follow the framework of the hybrid algorithm proposed by Wang et al., while allowing an arbitrary solving degree $d$ in the application of the XL algorithm. We further consider two variants: an XFL-based method that combines partial Gaussian elimination with variable guessing, and a WXL-based method that exploits the sparsity of the Macaulay matrix. Our complexity analysis for various parameter settings shows that, for some fixed values of $n$ and $k$, the WXL-based variant using a larger solving degree $d>2$ is particularly efficient when the block size $\beta$ is sufficiently small, while the original hybrid algorithm becomes more efficient as $\beta$ increases.

item.title: Accelerating Pollard Rho with GPU Field Arithmetic on NVIDIA Blackwell
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2469
Authors: Adam Buran, Kevin Nguyen
Summary: We show how far Pollard rho can be accelerated on current NVIDIA GPUs by rebuilding its field arithmetic around the hardware, with the Certicom challenge ECC2K-130, the Koblitz curve $y^2+xy=x^3+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{131}}$ with an expected cost of $2^{60.9}$ iterations, as the benchmark. None of the speedup comes from changing the algorithm. It comes from a packed normal-basis representation in which every Frobenius power is a permutation network instead of a chain of squarings; from the carry-less multiply that CUDA 13.3 exposes in PTX (clmad), which forms a 131-bit product in six instructions; from three-input logic instructions for everything around it; and from a batch size, launch geometry and compact tiled state chosen by measurement against the pipes they load. Across sixteen paired steps, each held to a rule written down before it ran, these take one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell from a $0.85$ billion iterations per second bitsliced control to $14.64$ in the audited campaign build, a $17.2\times$ gain (representation and arithmetic $6.3\times$, geometry $1.5\times$, memory layout $1.3\times$, clmad $1.2\times$), and a later build reaches $15.88$. That is about $230$ times the best published 2010 GPU kernel per card and puts the whole challenge under five GPU-years: five cards expect a solution within a year, a thousand in about three days. The gains depend on the die. clmad issues ten to eighteen times faster per SM-clock on the data-centre parts than on the workstation part, so the same change can win on one Blackwell part and lose on another; we report twelve GPUs from Turing to Blackwell per card, per SM and per dollar, and the CPU instruction sets that play the same role. Upper bounds derived from measured pipe rates leave about $1.5\times$ of headroom on one RTX PRO 6000, at $24$–$26$ billion iterations per second for any walk with one addition per step. The same levers applied to Pollard rho on NIST P-256 and P-384 on the same card give $1.52\times$ and $2.61\times$, to $1.632$ and $0.548$ billion iterations per second, which still leaves P-256 about $6\cdot10^{21}$ card-years away. We also separate the $\sigma$-walk from a table walk whose $20.08$ was measured under a cycle rule later found unsound (the exact rule runs at $8.24$), measure the walk constant at $2^{60.91}$–$2^{60.92}$ iterations, and report an FPGA engine at $8.25$ billion iterations per second on one AWS F2 and a campaign that walked $2^{56.68}$ iterations, $5.4\%$ of the expected work. Every number cites an evidence record; the code, data, evidence and a Dockerfile whose image starts the ECC2K-130 walk are at https://github.com/aburan28/rho-blackwell. None of this improves on the generic-group bound, and we do not claim that it does.

item.title: FlatMerkle: Logarithmic-Space Inclusion Proofs over a Single Linear Hash Stream
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2468
Authors: Sergio Demian Lerner
Summary: Merkle trees are the standard way to obtain logarithmic-size, logarithmic-time inclusion proofs over a large dataset, but they require a tree-shaped hash structure distinct from the ordinary, linear (Merkle--Damg\aa rd) hashing that most deployed systems -- including Bitcoin's own transaction and witness hashing -- actually perform. We present FlatMerkle, a construction that achieves the same asymptotic guarantees, $O(\log N)$ proof size and $O(\log N)$ verification time, over a single ordinary linear hash stream, by periodically re-injecting the hash function's own past internal states (``checkpoints'') back into the stream as ordinary message content. The result is a flat byte sequence whose digest is a single, unmodified invocation of the underlying hash function -- syntactically an ordinary digest of an ordinary byte string, not a distinguishable commitment format -- while still supporting compact inclusion proofs for any element, and compact proofs that a published file is malformed, so that an honest party can always answer a malicious committer in logarithmic space. We give the recursive construction, a closed-form formula locating any element in the structured stream, worked examples with illustrations, a security reduction to free-start collision resistance of the hash function's compression step, an optimal element-size analysis for both a flexible toy primitive and real SHA-256, a batched multi-element proof construction, a measured construction-speed comparison against Merkle trees, a concrete application to committing data inside a Bitcoin transaction annex (BIP-341), a design sketch using that application as a data-availability layer for an optimistic Bitcoin rollup, a from-scratch gas-cost comparison, on Ethereum, Rootstock, and Arbitrum, of an in-contract FlatMerkle commitment against an in-contract Merkle tree, tracing the three chains' differing verdicts to specific protocol design choices rather than to anything intrinsic to either construction, and a comparison against the closest prior art we are aware of, authenticated append-only skip lists.

item.title: DPF-SGD: Byzantine-Robust Differentially Private Federated SGD with Exact Optimality Guarantees
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2467
Authors: Likang Lu, Jiaxin Wu
Summary: Federated optimization enables collaborative learning over decentralized data but is accompanied by significant privacy risks due to the exchange of model updates. While differential privacy (DP) provides formal protection, optimization accuracy is often degraded, and robustness becomes particularly limited in the presence of Byzantine agents. A Byzantine-robust, differentially private federated SGD algorithm, DPF-SGD, is proposed, in which private step sizes are integrated with a DP noise–decay schedule to regulate gradient updates. To further enhance robustness, a privacy-preserving comparative elimination (PPCE) filter is developed to suppress Byzantine contributions during aggregation while preserving privacy guarantees. Almost sure convergence to the global optimum under ϵ-differential privacy is established, despite persistent noise and adversarial behavior. Experiments on synthetic and MNIST datasets demonstrate oneto two-order-of-magnitude reductions in final optimization error relative to DP baselines.

item.title: Trustless Bitcoin Vaults
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2466
Authors: Lukas Aumayr, Xinshu Dong, Runchao Han, Srivatsan Sridhar, David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani
Summary: Bitcoin (BTC) is the largest crypto asset, yet the Bitcoin blockchain offers few applications in which BTC can be used. A standard approach to make BTC useful is bridging: BTC is deposited on the Bitcoin chain and a wrapped asset is minted on a chain such as Ethereum, where it can be used in smart contract applications. Unfortunately, all Bitcoin bridges to date require trust assumptions on a centralized party or a committee running the bridge to enable withdrawals of the deposited BTC, including state-of-the-art BitVM bridges.
In this paper, we observe that while bridges are application-agnostic, most BTC holders are interested in collateral-based applications, where BTC is deposited as collateral, and only the depositor or a set of known counterparties can withdraw the asset. For this class of applications, we propose a primitive, Trustless Bitcoin Vaults, that guarantees that the BTC depositor or the counterparties can withdraw the deposited BTC following only the logic of the application smart contract without trusting any third party. We present a protocol that achieves the security guarantees of this primitive and instantiate it for a lending application where the deposited BTC is used as collateral to borrow against a set of liquidators on the Aave v4 smart contracts on Ethereum. Our mainnet experiments show that at the current Bitcoin price and fee rate, a deposit costs about \$0.7 in fees while a withdrawal costs at most \$7.7. Our construction is built on recent advances in efficient proof verification for Bitcoin.

item.title: Snapshots of TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Leak Plaintext Histograms via Dendrochronology
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2465
Authors: Zachary Espiritu
Summary: The paper is currently under embargo and will be released by the end of October 2026.

item.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2464
Authors: Souvik Das, Ariful Azad, Nitesh Saxena
Summary: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

item.title: Tree-BTE: Batched Threshold Encryption using Additive Homomorphism
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2463
Authors: Amit Agarwal, Sourav Das, Babak Poorebrahim Gilkalaye, Benny Pinkas, Peter Rindal
Summary: Batched threshold encryption (BTE) enables a committee of servers to jointly decrypt any chosen subset of ciphertexts from a large pool, while all remaining ciphertexts stay private. BTE is a key building block for encrypted mempools, where transactions are encrypted until block inclusion to mitigate maximal extractable value (MEV). We give a new tree-based BTE construction from two simple building blocks which support additive homomorphism: a symmetric-key encryption scheme that is homomorphic over key and message space, and a thresholdizable public-key encryption scheme that is homomorphic over message space. These building blocks can be instantiated under a wide variety of assumptions including DDH, DCR, LWR and even LWE for post-quantum security.
In our scheme, each ciphertext is associated with an index from an appropriate index space. We implement the DDH-based instantiation. Given an aggregated batch of 1,000 messages over a small 1024 sized index space, each server performs about 41~ms of single-thread computation, including a 100-of-300 threshold decryption. We also partially implement an RLWE-based post-quantum instantiation over a \(2^{128}\) sized index space for negligible collision probability among indices. A batch of 1024 messages uses approximately 0.89 MB per ciphertext and 20 seconds of single-thread decryption per server.

item.title: Hybrid Quantum–Computational Key Distribution with Reduced Assumptions (Short Paper)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2462
Authors: Jean Snyman, Ioana Boureanu, Daniel Gardham
Summary: The HM-QCT protocol, presented by Mazzoncini et al. in 2025, uses a unique feature of quantum information to achieve quantum key distribution (QKD) with secret-key rates beyond standard constructions. The protocol has been designed in the hybrid quantum–computational time-lock (QCT) security model which imposes two independent (but related) restrictions on the attacker: (1) a computationally secure encryption scheme which a successful attacker must break within a narrow timeframe and (2) an assumption that the attacker can only store quantum information with low fidelity.
We first review the protocol and its two-assumption model by presenting, in explicit form, the two natural “harvest now, decrypt later” strategies against it, one using quantum memory and one using classical memory. We show how each is excluded by exactly one of the two assumptions, so that harvesting resistance rests on their conjunction and on the presumed existence of a technological gap: the adversary's quantum memory must decohere much faster than the time it takes to break the short-term encryption.
Finally, we introduce HM-PRF, a variant that replaces the short-term encryption with a pseudorandom function (PRF), evaluated locally. By eliminating the transmission of enciphered classical information, the adversary does not need to race an impending expiry event. We compare the security of our construction against the original and argue that our PRF-based assumption yields a more realistic adversary. It simply requires the existence of one-way functions rather than a predicted lasting limitation of quantum computation and memory technology.

item.title: Leakage-Resilient Incompressible Cryptography: Constructions and Barriers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2461
Authors: KAARTIK BHUSHAN, Rishab Goyal, Venkata Koppula, Varun Narayanan, Manoj Prabhakaran, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree
Summary: We introduce Leakage-Resilient Incompressible cryptography, which simultaneously addresses two variants of side-channel attacks that have been tackled in theoretical cryptography. Leakage-resilience seeks to provide security against an adversary who learns a part of the secret-key and the entire ciphertext or signature; conversely, incompressible cryptography provides security against an adversary who learns the entire secret-key, but only a part of the ciphertext or signature. However, constructions in either of these security models can fail against an attack in the other model. In this work, we define a new model of security that subsumes both leakage-resilient cryptography and incompressible cryptography, and we present several non-trivial positive and negative results.
On the positive side, first we present a transformation from incompressible symmetric-key encryption (SKE) to leakage-resilient incompressible SKE in the information-theoretic setting. Next, as one of our main results, we construct a leakage-resilient incompressible public-key encryption (PKE), combining an incompressible SKE and a new primitive that we call leakage-resilient non-committing key encapsulation mechanism (LR-NC-KEM).
While an information-theoretic incompressible SKE suitable for use in both these constructions already exists in the literature (Dziembowski, CRYPTO 2006), we present a new construction achieving ciphertext-rate $\frac{1}{2}$ and compression-rate $\frac{1}{2}$, using an appropriate notion of invertible extractors; this leads to corresponding improvements in the final parameters we obtain in these constructions. We also construct a leakage-resilient incompressible signature scheme in the classical random oracle model, assuming $(\mathsf{DCR}\text{ or }\mathsf{LWE})$ and the Decisional Linear assumption, with signature-rate and compression-rate $1-o(1)$ and leakage-rate $1$.
On the negative side, we show barriers to significantly improving the parameters we obtain, by showing impossibility of basing the security of such improved schemes on blackbox reductions.
Apart from the general framework and the specific results we obtain, some of the intermediate tools that we define and instantiate, like LR-NC-KEM and invertible extractors, may be of independent interest.

item.title: Cube Attacks with Elimination Strategy: Key Recovery Attacks on Trivium
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2460
Authors: Haoran Li, Shichang Wang, Meicheng Liu, Willi Meier, Dongdai Lin
Summary: In this paper, we present a novel framework for cube attacks named cube attacks with elimination strategy. The core idea is to find specific key conditions and cubes such that their superpolies under these key conditions can be efficiently computed. By recovering these conditional superpolies, we can solve the corresponding equation system and thereby retrieve key information. If a sufficient number of such key conditions can be found, the attack can be extended to a larger key space. To apply this framework in practical attacks, we propose the following techniques.
First, we propose a nested coefficient solver that combines variable substitution and symbolic computation to efficiently recover superpolies, and present the conditional monomial prediction technique to rapidly recover conditional superpolies. Second, by combining numeric mapping with monomial prediction techniques, we propose an automated cube search algorithm that is capable of generating a large number of good cubes for attacks. Finally, we develop two kinds of testing methods, which are used to efficiently extract substantial key information from large-scale equation systems.
To illustrate the power of our techniques, we apply them to Trivium. As a result, for 840 rounds of Trivium, a practical key recovery attack is mounted with complexity below $2^{55}$ and a success rate 77.8\%. For 845 rounds, we present a practical key recovery attack with complexity below $2^{56}$ and a success rate 98.1\% for $2^{80} \times 59.1\%$ keys. For 855 rounds, we present a theoretical weak-key recovery attack for $2^{74}$ keys. To the best of our knowledge, these are the best practical and theoretical attacks on Trivium. The improvements in the number of rounds reached are 13 for practical attacks and 4 for theoretical attacks, respectively.

item.title: Causal Awareness in End-to-End Encrypted Group Messaging
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2459
Authors: Joseph Jaeger, Akshaya Kumar, Igors Stepanovs
Summary: Chats do not always unfold in a single clear order. Two users may send messages before information about either message reaches the other sender. Such messages are concurrent, but most instant messengers provide no way for users to recognize this relationship. Chen and Fischlin (Eurocrypt 2024) studied this limitation in the two-user setting, showing that Signal does not expose enough information to recover the context in which a message was sent; they proposed a fix. We study group chats, where a user may need to reason about ordering and concurrency among other users' messages. This can become a security problem when network delays or adversarial interference cause an authentic message to be shown in a misleading context.
Event ordering is a classical problem; Lamport clocks and vector clocks are standard starting points. Secure messaging needs a different treatment because communication is asynchronous, bandwidth is limited, and added latency is undesirable. To address the problem under these constraints, we introduce causal awareness: the ability of a receiver to reconstruct a specified part of the causal context in which an accepted message was sent. Senders transmit records of what they have sent and received. Receivers verify these records and compare them with their own.
We develop a framework of correctness and security notions for causal awareness in group chats. Our definitions are parameterized by how much causal information receivers must recover. We give baseline constructions and prove their properties. We also introduce checkpoint-aided and server-aided variants of the framework and prove that, in each, our notions of correctness and integrity imply causal awareness. We discuss how causal information could be surfaced in a messenger's user interface.

item.title: Master-Key Recovery from Internal Activation Leakage in ReLU Realizations of Camellia
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2458
Authors: Kwangjo Kim
Summary: This paper investigates functional correctness and masterkey reconstruction in explicitly constructed rectified linear unit (ReLU) implementations of Camellia-128, Camellia-192, and Camellia-256. Exact neural realizations of Boolean gates, S-box selectors, and bit permutations provide a framework for reproducing Camellia on binary inputs. We present a component-wise correctness argument and report known-answer-test agreement for Camellia-128. We then analyze how selected whitening and round-key quantities determine the external master key through public key-schedule identities. Inverse rotations of suitable subkey pairs recover the required key components, whereas prewhitening-key recovery alone is insufficient for complete reconstruction of the longer keys. Under explicitly constructed synthetic internal-oracle access, symmetric real-valued perturbations identify target subkey bits, requiring 128 and 256 query pairs for the coordinate-wise Camellia-128 and Camellia-256 procedures, respectively. A separate Camellia-192 experiment validates deterministic key-schedule inversion under direct access to DNN-generated round keys. Across 1,000 independently sampled master keys per variant, all three procedures achieved exact recovery in every trial, yielding 3,000 successful recoveries out of 3,000 trials, with zero recovery failures and no Camellia-192 complement-consistency failures. These results validate conditional master-key reconstruction under the specified internal-access models and highlight the distinction between binary functional correctness and security under stronger access assumptions. They do not establish plaintext/ciphertext-only attacks against standard Camellia.

item.title: On Secure Sorting and Its Application to Privacy-Preserving Graph Pattern Matching
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2457
Authors: Marcel Keller
Summary: Sorting in secure computation has been studied almost as long as there have been implementations of multi-party computation (Wang et al., AsiaCCS'10). More recent advances include completely secure implementations (revealing nothing other than the list size) that have used Quicksort (Araki et al., CCS'21) and radix sort (Asharov et al., CCS'22). For the first time, we extensively compare the two variants across a range of parameters and for both honest- and dishonest-majority computation. We then apply secure sorting to improve sparse matrix multiplication without oblivious RAM based on recent work by Damie et al. (CODASPY'26). Our main contribution here is to produce an output in the same format as the inputs to the multiplication. This is needed for repeated multiplication of graph adjacency matrices, which we use to find cycles in graphs. Such cycles have been associated with money laundering, and this also applies to another graph pattern dubbed scatter-gather, which we can detect with the same approach. Our work therefore can be applied to privacy-preserving anti-money laundering detection.

item.title: On the Expected Number of Iterations in ML-DSA Signing: A Complete Accounting of the Rejection Conditions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2456
Authors: Kris Kwiatkowski
Summary: FIPS 204 Table 1 gives the expected number of iterations of the ML-DSA signing loop (ML-DSA.Sign_internal, Algorithm 7), citing CRYSTALS-Dilithium Equation (5). That equation covers only the validity checks on line 23 ($\lVert z \rVert_\infty$ and $\lVert r_0 \rVert_\infty$) and omits the two encoding-correctness checks on line 28 ($\lVert c \cdot t_0 \rVert_\infty$ and the hint weight), a scoping distinction the Dilithium specification states explicitly and FIPS 204 does not reproduce. We give a complete accounting of all four conditions. The $z$ check on line 23 is computed exactly by counting; the $c \cdot t_0$ term follows a closed-form Irwin-Hall tail, restating a peer-reviewed result by Yan, Luo and Wang; the hint-weight term's per-coefficient probability, conditioned on line 23 having passed, does have a closed form, but the tail of the sum over $256k$ such coefficients does not, since their probabilities are unequal, random, and correlated with each other, so we give the conditioned per-coefficient probability in closed form and estimate its tail by Monte Carlo. The corrected expected iteration counts are 4.36, 5.14 and 3.91 for ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87, matching a real end-to-end measurement to within 0.14% and already reflected in NIST's own errata to FIPS 204.

item.title: CUTS: Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2455
Authors: Jamie Judd, Louis Tajan, Conor Deegan, Furkan Akal
Summary: Stateful hash-based signatures fail badly when a one-time key signs twice, as happens when the signer's state is lost or rolled back. We study what a second signature reveals in a broad class of hash-based schemes whose key is a tree of hash chains. In this class, a message selects a set of tree nodes that covers every leaf exactly once, together with a position on the chain of each selected node, and the signature reveals the chain values at those positions. For the whole class, we prove that the values derivable from several signatures are exactly the union of those derivable from each signature alone, and we bound forgery after $b$ signatures in the classical random-oracle model by a combinatorial coverage exponent $\lambda_b$, also when the signer grinds a counter. We then present CUTS (Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures), a member of the class built on one binary tree, in which both the selected nodes and their chain positions depend on the message, with the positions summing to a fixed value $S$. Signature length and verification cost are fixed by the parameters and do not depend on the tree height. For CUTS, we compute the two-use coverage exactly as one coefficient of a polynomial and derive deterministic lower bounds on $\lambda_2$; one parameter set with 1 424-byte signatures has $\lambda_2\ge128.6$. A counter variant, CUTS+C, trades a short counter and extra signing work for a proven grinding gain of $g$ bits in the coverage term.

item.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2454
Authors: Hai H. Nguyen
Summary: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following.
(1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$.
(2) For every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+\delta)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\frac{\delta}{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $\delta$.
(3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $\eta_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $\eta_c>0$.
All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.

item.title: Revisiting Witness-Succinct UC-lifting Compilers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2453
Authors: Davide Li Calsi, Luigi Russo, Dominique Schröder, Federico Valbusa
Summary: Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are increasingly used within larger cryptographic protocols, making security under composition essential. Generic compilation to Universal Composability (UC) requires straight-line, black-box extraction while preserving succinctness and controlling prover cost.
We introduce verifiable reconstructible straightline codes (VRSCs), a primitive that separates public hiding, transcript-based reconstruction, binding, and proof non-rerandomizability. This abstraction exposes a missing security requirement in the witness-succinct UC compiler of Ganesh et al. (EUROCRYPT 2023). Permuting previously revealed evaluation openings produces a fresh accepting proof with non-negligible probability without violating non-extrapolation, invalidating the claimed simulation argument. Proof non-rerandomizability captures this attack at the certificate level. Our construction prevents transfers between repetitions through verifier-enforced disjoint evaluation domains.
We formulate a generic UC lifting theorem in terms of VRSCs and give a pairing-based instantiation using a Fischlin-style search over authenticated codeword symbols. Structured Reed--Solomon encoding and jointly computed KZG openings reduce certificate-generation work from quadratic to \(O_{\lambda}(n\log n)\), where \(n\) is the witness size. Only a linear-time encoding check enters the underlying SNARK circuit. To our knowledge, this is the first generic UC lifting compiler that simultaneously achieves quasi-linear prover overhead and constant additional proof size and verification work with respect to the witness size.

item.title: Genericity in multivariate cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2452
Authors: Simon Abelard, Pierre Pébereau, Mohab Safey El Din
Summary: The results in this paper establish the genericity of some properties of the ideals and varieties generated by UOV public keys, in particular the equidimensionality of the UOV varieties and the radicality of public key ideals. These genericity results justify the various regularity assumptions that are made on polynomial systems of equations arising in the cryptanalysis of UOV and its variants. We also provide examples in the recent literature showing how genericity questions arise in crypt- analysis and why genericity should be taken into consideration when de- signing cryptographic schemes. Lastly, we perform a retrospective study of various cryptographic schemes through the viewangle of genericity. We identify several cases in which non-genericity led to the cryptanaly- sis of the scheme, but also provide a counter-example of a scheme whose non-genericity does not seem easy to exploit.

item.title: Extended biprojective APN functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2451
Authors: Nadiia Ichanska, Nikolay Kaleyski
Summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions provide optimal resistance to differential cryptanalysis in characteristic two, and constructing new infinite families inequivalent to the known ones remains an important problem in the study of cryptographic functions. We introduce extended biprojective functions, obtained by augmenting biprojective polynomials with truncated trace terms, and establish a new infinite family of quadratic APN functions. To investigate these constructions, we develop an efficient APN test based on the ranks of binary matrices and employ it in exhaustive searches in dimensions up to 28. Using ortho-derivative differential spectra to distinguish CCZ-equivalence classes, we identify APN functions inequivalent to known families and uncover a systematic pattern across dimensions, leading to conjectures on further infinite families of quadratic APN functions.

item.title: Modulus Operandi: Round-Optimal Modulus Conversion for MPC and Threshold FHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2450
Authors: Ivan Damgård, Sebastian Hasler, Sebastian Kolby, Stanislas Pawlak
Summary: In secure multiparty computation (MPC), modulus conversion turns a sharing of a value $x$ modulo $q$ into a sharing of the same value modulo $t$, without leaking anything about $x$. One important application of modulus conversion is in threshold decryption for lattice-based cryptosystems, where a sharing modulo the ciphertext modulus has to be moved to the plaintext modulus before it can be opened. The most efficient protocols so far (Damgård et al., Asiacrypt 2026) are in the preprocessing model, assume $x$ is bounded away from $q$ by a constant factor and take two rounds for a prime target modulus, three rounds for arbitrary moduli, and one round when all moduli are 2-powers. We improve upon this by constructing three new modulus conversion protocols in the preprocessing model:
- Our first conversion protocol takes a single round for arbitrary moduli, consisting of just one opening. - Our second conversion protocol is a variant of the first protocol, where in the preprocessing most of the secure multiplications are replaced by private inputs, which are checked in a batch using fully linear interactive oracle proofs (FLIOPs). This makes the preprocessing cheaper (amortized over a batch of conversions) when the number $N$ of parties is small. This comes at the cost of making the bound on $x$ a factor $N$ stronger. - Our third conversion protocol avoids the bound on $x$ altogether but takes two rounds.
All our protocols are stated in the arithmetic black box (ABB) model, so they can run on top of a wide variety of MPC protocols, inheriting their corruption threshold and security model.
To allow the third conversion protocol to run in two rounds, we construct the first one-round comparison protocol in the ABB model for comparing a bitwise shared $n$-bit value against a public threshold with polynomial-size preprocessing. Concretely, the preprocessing size is $\mathcal O(n^2)$ in general, and $\mathcal O(n^2 / \log n)$ in our case where the secret value is fixed in preprocessing.
We also construct constant-round ABB protocols without preprocessing for computing symmetric functions and comparisons of values shared bitwise modulo powers of arbitrary primes (e.g., $2^k$), at communication quasi-linear in the number of input bits. Previously, this required either a sufficiently large prime or polynomially larger communication.
Finally, we give an impossibility result for non-interactive modulus conversion, demonstrating that a single round is optimal: unless $t$ divides $q$, every non-interactive conversion for inputs $x < q/\beta$ is incorrect with probability at least $\approx 1/(4\beta)$.

item.title: Optimal Threshold Implementations of all bijective 4-bit S-boxes and new Infinite Families
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2449
Authors: Enrico Piccione, Yevhen Perehuda, Gregor Leander, Patrick Felke
Summary: Threshold implementations (TIs) are now an established class of side-channel countermeasures. Their underlying idea is simple and compelling: under mild, practical assumptions, they provide protection against glitches and allow composability. Yet our understanding of one-stage TIs with a minimal number of shares remains limited, both for cryptographically relevant families—particularly power functions—and for concrete small functions. In particular, until now, except for Feistel-constructions, no optimal TI had been found for families of mathematically well-structured and cryptographically non-trivial functions, especially power functions. In small dimensions, many functions - particularly cryptographically interesting ones — were not known to admit an optimal TI. This was especially true for the 4-bit S-boxes frequently used in practical lightweight ciphers. Optimal refers to share-optimal, direct one-stage, uniform, first-order TI. Here, we introduce new families of TIs, including the first infinite families of cryptographically nontrivial power permutations.
